disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Linux-first security concepts in the Hackers-Arise tradition; not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Hackers-Arise or any Linux distribution. Practice only on systems you own. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

choices: It's fine — root login is convenient for admins
Disable root SSH login, enforce key-based auth, and change the default port only as obscurity-plus — keys and no-root are the real controls
Just make the root password longer
Disable SSH entirely and use telnet
scenarios.hint: Which of these settings lets an attacker even attempt to guess the most powerful account?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong, and what is the correct hardening?
scenarios.situation: A fresh VPS has this SSH config. It's already getting thousands of login attempts per day.
scenarios.title: The wide-open SSH
scenarios.why: PermitRootLogin yes plus password auth is the classic initial-access gift: attackers brute-force root directly. Key-based auth removes the guessable secret; disabling root login removes the highest-value target. Port changes are obscurity, not security — fine as a supplement, useless as a strategy.

choices: chmod 777 so the app can always write
Set ownership to the app user, 640/750 permissions, and investigate why the app needs broader access — fix the cause, not the symptom
Move the file to /tmp where permissions don't matter
Run the app as root so permissions never block it
scenarios.hint: Who can read this file right now — and who actually needs to?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
scenarios.situation: An app config containing a database password is world-readable. The app runs as user 'webapp.'
scenarios.title: The readable secret
scenarios.why: World-readable secrets are a finding, not a convenience. Least privilege: only the app user (and root) should read it — 640 owned by webapp, or 600. chmod 777 and running as root both trade a permission error for a systemic vulnerability. Fix the access need properly instead of opening the file to everyone.

choices: Uninstall the package manager to prevent changes
Apply security updates on a tested schedule, prioritize internet-facing services, and have a rollback plan — unpatched CVEs are the top initial-access vector
Only patch when there's a breach
Patching breaks things; disable auto-updates forever
scenarios.hint: What do most successful initial-access attacks exploit — zero-days, or known patches nobody applied?
scenarios.prompt: What is the professional patching posture?
scenarios.situation: A server hasn't been updated in 14 months. The admin fears patches will break the app.
scenarios.title: Fourteen months behind
scenarios.why: The overwhelming majority of exploited vulnerabilities are known CVEs with available patches — 'patch fear' is how servers get owned. The professional answer is process: test updates, schedule them, prioritize exposed services, and keep rollback capability. Unpatched is not stable; it's just vulnerable quietly.

choices: Leave it — it's probably needed
Audit listening services, disable what isn't required, and firewall the rest — every listener is attack surface
Only worry about services on port 80
Reinstall the OS to be safe
scenarios.hint: For each listener, ask: who needs to reach this, and from where?
scenarios.prompt: What is the hardening workflow here?
scenarios.situation: A server exposes telnet, MySQL, and an old Tomcat to the whole internet. It's supposed to be a web server.
scenarios.title: Too many open doors
scenarios.why: Every listening service is attack surface, and telnet (cleartext) plus an old Tomcat are classic footholds. Hardening means: inventory listeners, remove what's unneeded, bind the rest to localhost or internal interfaces, and firewall what's left. 'Probably needed' is not an answer — verify or remove.

choices: Give the intern the root password — it's faster
Create a personal account, add a scoped sudo rule for exactly the commands needed, and require the intern's own password for sudo
Add the intern to the sudo group with ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
Share your own account — you'll change the password later
scenarios.hint: What happens when this intern leaves — and what can you audit with each option?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct approach?
scenarios.situation: An intern needs to restart the web service and view logs — nothing else.
scenarios.title: The intern needs sudo
scenarios.why: Sudo exists for precisely this: delegate specific privileges to named individuals with audit trails. ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD for an intern is a standing root equivalent with no accountability. Scoped rules (exact commands), personal accounts, and password-required sudo give least privilege plus attribution — and clean revocation when the internship ends.

choices: It's fine — convenience for the team
Find and remove them: scan authorized_keys across accounts, require key approval, and investigate how they got there
Add more keys so everyone has access
Keys don't expire so there's nothing to do
evidence:
ssh-rsa AAAAB3... former-employee-laptop
ssh-rsa AAAAB3... unknown-key-2023
scenarios.hint: Whose keys are these, and who approved each one?
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk, and the fix?
scenarios.situation: The root account's authorized_keys contains keys for a former employee and an unidentified key.
scenarios.title: Ghost keys
scenarios.why: Stale SSH keys are persistent, unaudited access — the former employee's laptop may be long gone but the key still opens root. SSH key hygiene means: inventory keys per account, tie each to an approved identity, remove leavers promptly, and consider key expiry or certificates. 'Unknown-key-2023' on root is an incident until proven otherwise.

choices: Block all outbound traffic — servers don't need the internet
Default-deny inbound, allow only required ports from required sources; allow established/related; log and review drops
Allow all inbound — the app needs to be reachable
Firewalls are obsolete with encryption
scenarios.hint: What should the firewall do with a packet nobody asked for?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct firewall posture for this server?
scenarios.situation: You're firewalling a web server that needs 80/443 from anywhere and 22 from the office IP only.
scenarios.title: The firewall ruleset
scenarios.why: Default-deny with explicit allows is the only sane firewall posture: every open port is a deliberate decision, and the stateful established/related rule keeps return traffic working without opening inbound holes. SSH restricted to the office IP shrinks the brute-force surface to near zero. 'Allow all, block bad' is unmaintainable.

choices: It's normal — DNS is chatty
Investigate: unexpected DNS to an unknown resolver can indicate tunneling or C2; check which process is querying and what the query patterns look like
Block port 53 entirely
Restart the DNS service
scenarios.hint: Why would a workstation bypass the corporate resolver — and what's encoded in those subdomains?
scenarios.prompt: What does this capture suggest, and what's your next step?
scenarios.situation: Packet capture on a workstation shows DNS queries to an external resolver (not the corporate one) with high-entropy subdomain labels.
scenarios.title: Reading the packets
scenarios.why: Direct-to-external DNS bypasses corporate monitoring — and high-entropy labels are the DNS tunneling signature. The capture tells you what logs might not: the actual query content and the rogue resolver. Next: identify the process, check query volume/patterns, and compare against the host's baseline. Packet truth beats assumption.

choices: Trust it — the tool is authoritative
Verify independently: check with ss/netstat, confirm the process binary path and hash, and investigate unexpected listeners — tools can be fooled by rootkits
Only check port 80 — that's what matters
Reinstall the monitoring tool
scenarios.hint: If an attacker owned this box, which of your tools would they lie to first?
scenarios.prompt: How do you verify what's really listening?
scenarios.situation: Your monitoring says only ports 80/443 are open, but external scans show port 4444 listening.
scenarios.title: The hidden listener
scenarios.why: A discrepancy between internal tooling and external observation is a classic rootkit indicator — userland tools can be hooked to hide processes and ports. Verify from multiple vantage points: external scan (ground truth for reachability), /proc inspection, and known-good binaries. When the box disagrees with the network, trust the network and investigate the box.

choices: It's encrypted so it's fine

ARP spoofing/poisoning lets an attacker position as man-in-the-middle on the LAN; use static ARP entries or dynamic ARP inspection where available, and prefer encrypted protocols so interception yields nothing
ARP is a WAN protocol — not a LAN concern
Disable ARP on the network
scenarios.hint: What does ARP trust by default — and what happens when someone lies about who owns the gateway's IP?
scenarios.prompt: What is the attack, and the defense?
scenarios.situation: On a shared office LAN, you demonstrate intercepting a colleague's traffic (with permission, in a lab) by answering ARP requests for the gateway.
scenarios.title: Poisoning the neighborhood
scenarios.why: ARP has no authentication — whoever answers first wins, so an attacker can redirect LAN traffic through themselves. Defenses are layered: switches with dynamic ARP inspection, static ARP for critical hosts, and above all encrypted protocols (SSH/HTTPS) so intercepted traffic is useless. The lab demo teaches why cleartext on LANs is a finding.

choices: Segment them: put IoT on an isolated VLAN with no access to the server VLAN, firewall between segments, and monitor the IoT segment as untrusted
It's fine — they're on the same switch as everything else
Just change the cameras' passwords
VLANs are only for large enterprises
scenarios.hint: What's the blast radius when (not if) a camera gets compromised?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct network design?
scenarios.situation: The office has 30 cheap IP cameras on the same flat network as the file server and workstations.
scenarios.title: Cameras on the LAN
scenarios.why: IoT devices are unpatchable, credential-stuffed, and historically botnetted — they must be treated as hostile. Segmentation (isolated VLAN, firewall rules denying IoT→server traffic, monitoring) contains the inevitable compromise. Password changes help but don't fix unpatchable firmware; flat networks turn one camera into a pivot to everything.

choices: Ping the host — if it replies, the port is open
Use a proper scan with service detection, but first confirm authorization and rate-limit it; interpret 'filtered' vs 'closed' correctly
Port scan from your phone to avoid detection
Scanning is illegal in all cases
scenarios.hint: What does 'filtered' tell you that 'closed' doesn't — and why does authorization come before the first packet?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct, professional approach to mapping open ports?
scenarios.situation: You need to audit which ports are reachable on a client's server from the internet.
scenarios.title: Mapping the perimeter
scenarios.why: 'Filtered' (no response — firewall dropping) vs 'closed' (RST — host reachable, port shut) tells you about firewall posture, not just services. Professional scanning means: written authorization first, rate limits to avoid DoS, service detection for fingerprinting, and honest reporting of what each state implies. Scanning without authorization is the line between audit and attack.

choices: It's fine — rm is fast
Quote variables, check the variable is set and non-empty before rm -rf, and use -- to guard against filenames starting with dashes
Use sudo to make sure it works
Delete is delete — no script can be safe
scenarios.hint: What is $BACKUP_DIR if the config file failed to load?
scenarios.prompt: What is the bug, and the fix?
scenarios.situation: A cleanup script deleted the wrong directory last night. This is the script.
scenarios.title: The rm -rf incident
scenarios.why: Unquoted, unchecked variables in rm -rf are how disasters happen: an empty $BACKUP_DIR turns the command into 'rm -rf /old/*' — or worse. Defensive scripting: set -u (fail on unset), quote everything, validate variables before destructive commands, and test with echo first. The script didn't malfunction; it did exactly what it was told.

choices: grep -i 'failed' /var/log/auth.log
A loop that parses timestamps, counts failures per IP in the window, and only reports IPs over threshold with first/last seen — then you review before blocking
Block every IP with a single failed login
Email the log to yourself daily
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between 'an IP failed once' and 'an attack is underway'?
scenarios.prompt: What should the script actually do?
scenarios.situation: You want a script to watch auth.log for SSH brute forcing and alert you.
scenarios.title: Watching the logs
scenarios.why: A useful monitor aggregates: per-IP counts within a time window, thresholds to separate attacks from typos, and first/last-seen timestamps for context. Alerting on every single failure is noise; auto-blocking without review risks self-DoS. The script's job is to turn raw logs into a decision-ready summary — the human still decides.

choices: Make it idempotent: check state first (is the rule already there? is the package installed?), so re-runs converge instead of duplicating
Run it twice to be sure
Idempotency is only for Ansible, not bash
Add 'set -x' and call it done
evidence:
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
useradd auditor
scenarios.hint: What happens the second time this runs — and the tenth?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with running this hardening script repeatedly?
scenarios.situation: Your hardening script appends a firewall rule and creates a user. Run twice, it errors and duplicates the rule.
scenarios.title: Run it twice
scenarios.why: Automation that isn't idempotent becomes a liability: duplicate firewall rules, failed user creation, unpredictable state. Check-before-change (iptables -C, id username) makes re-runs safe and convergent — the script describes desired state, not just actions. This is the foundational discipline behind all configuration management.

choices: It's fine — internal tool
Validate and sanitize: check the IP format, reject shell metacharacters, and prefer subprocess with argument lists over shell=True
Only allow admins to use it
Python is safe from injection by default
evidence:
import subprocess
target = input('Target: ')
subprocess.run(f'nmap {target}', shell=True)
scenarios.hint: What happens when the 'target' is '127.0.0.1; rm -rf /'?
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability in this helper script?
scenarios.situation: You wrote a Python wrapper around nmap for the team. It takes a target from input.
scenarios.title: The helpful wrapper
scenarios.why: shell=True with unsanitized input is command injection — the 'target' field becomes arbitrary shell. Even internal tools get abused or fed unexpected input. Fix: validate the input is actually an IP/hostname, and use subprocess with a list (no shell) so arguments can't become commands. Security tools must be secure tools.

choices: Run it as root from your home directory — cron handles the rest
Use absolute paths, minimal environment, lock files to prevent overlap, log output, and run with the least privilege needed
Cron is deprecated — use sleep loops instead
Put passwords in the script — cron is secure
scenarios.hint: What environment does cron provide — and what happens when the 5-minute job takes 7 minutes?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a cron job production-safe?
scenarios.situation: Your backup script runs every 5 minutes from cron but fails silently half the time.
scenarios.title: The flaky cron job
scenarios.why: Cron's minimal environment (bare PATH, no shell profile) breaks scripts that work interactively — absolute paths fix that. Overlapping runs corrupt backups — lock files (flock) fix that. Silent failures hide for months — logging and alerting fix that. And the job should run as the least-privileged user that can do the work, with secrets from a vault, never hardcoded.

choices: curl the URL and pipe to bash — it's the documented install
Download the installer, verify its checksum/signature against the vendor's published value over a separate channel, then run it
Piping to bash is fine on HTTPS
Only install from apt — never use vendor scripts
scenarios.hint: What does HTTPS prove about the file — and what doesn't it prove?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe way to handle this?
scenarios.situation: A vendor's docs say: curl https://vendor.example/install.sh | sudo bash.
scenarios.title: Pipe to shell
scenarios.why: HTTPS proves the connection wasn't tampered with in transit — it proves nothing about whether the vendor's server was compromised or the docs were hijacked. Verifying a published checksum or signature (fetched separately) before executing is the minimum due diligence. curl|bash as a habit trains you to execute uninspected code as root — the exact behavior attackers rely on.

choices: Encrypt the passwords with AES so they can be decrypted later
Hash with a slow, salted password-hashing function (bcrypt/argon2); never store reversible passwords
Store them in plaintext — the DB is internal
MD5 is fine — it's a hash
scenarios.hint: What should happen when the database leaks — and which option survives that?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct design?
scenarios.situation: You're reviewing an app that stores user passwords 'encrypted' with a key in the config file.
scenarios.title: Storing passwords
scenarios.why: Passwords must be hashed with purpose-built slow functions (bcrypt, argon2) with unique salts — 'encrypted' passwords are just plaintext with extra steps once the key leaks (and the key is always next to the data). Fast hashes (MD5/SHA-256) fall to GPUs in hours. Design for the breach: the stored value must be useless to the attacker who steals it.

choices: They're the same — both scramble data
Hashing is one-way (integrity/identity); encryption is reversible (confidentiality). Use each for its purpose: hash to verify, encrypt to protect
Encryption is always stronger
Hashing is encryption with a fixed key
scenarios.hint: If you need the original data back later, which one did you need?
scenarios.prompt: A teammate uses the terms interchangeably. What is the correct distinction?
scenarios.situation: 'We hashed the backups so nobody can read them,' a teammate says.
scenarios.title: Hash is not encryption
scenarios.why: This confusion causes real design failures: hashed backups are still readable by everyone (hashing doesn't hide data); 'encrypted' passwords are recoverable. Hashing proves integrity and identity (this file hasn't changed); encryption provides confidentiality (only key holders can read). Using the wrong primitive means the security property you wanted doesn't exist.

choices: Generate it with the OS CSPRNG (/dev/urandom, secrets module) and protect it like the data it guards — keys in code/config repos are compromised keys
Use the current timestamp as the key
Hardcode it — the repo is private
Email it to the team for backup
scenarios.hint: What is the attacker's first stop when hunting for keys?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct key lifecycle for this app?
scenarios.situation: Your app needs an encryption key for API tokens. A teammate suggests hardcoding it in the repo.
scenarios.title: Where do keys live?
scenarios.why: Keys in repos get leaked (history, forks, breaches) and timestamps aren't random. Correct practice: generate with a cryptographically secure RNG, store in a proper secrets manager or environment-provided vault, rotate on schedule and on personnel changes, and never commit. The key's protection must match the data's value — the key IS the security.

choices: It's fine — the cert is just a formality
Investigate: cert errors mean the connection's identity can't be verified — possible misconfiguration or interception; never click through on sensitive systems
Click through — you need to get work done
Certs only matter for public websites
scenarios.hint: What is the certificate actually vouching for — and what does an error mean about that vouch?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
scenarios.situation: Your browser warns about the certificate on the company's internal admin panel.
scenarios.title: The certificate warning
scenarios.why: A cert warning means the identity check failed — the server might be misconfigured, expired, or an attacker's. Clicking through trains the exact habit attackers exploit and is never acceptable for admin panels. The fix is operational: proper internal CA or valid certs, renewed before expiry, with monitoring. Warnings are the system working; ignoring them is the failure.

choices: Email the file — it's faster
Sign the file with your private key and share the signature; recipients verify with your public key — but first they must authenticate your public key through a trusted channel
Encryption and signing are the same thing
Just tell them the SHA256 over the phone
scenarios.hint: What stops an attacker from sending their own file with their own valid signature?
scenarios.prompt: How do you prove the file really came from you?
scenarios.situation: You need to send a critical config file to a remote admin and prove it wasn't tampered with.
scenarios.title: Proving it's really from you
scenarios.why: Signing proves integrity and origin — but only if the recipient has YOUR authentic public key. An attacker can sign anything with their own key; the security is in the key distribution (verified fingerprint, trusted introducer, prior secure exchange). Signatures without authenticated keys are theater. Get the trust bootstrap right.

choices: Symmetric — one key is simpler
Asymmetric for the key exchange, symmetric for the data — this hybrid is what TLS and GPG actually do, because symmetric is fast and asymmetric solves key distribution
Asymmetric for everything — it's more secure
It doesn't matter
scenarios.hint: What is each one good at — and what is each one bad at?
scenarios.prompt: You must design encryption for large backups sent to a partner. Which approach?
scenarios.situation: You need confidentiality for multi-gigabyte backup transfers to a partner org.
scenarios.title: Choosing the cipher
scenarios.why: Real systems are hybrid: asymmetric crypto (slow, solves key distribution) exchanges a random symmetric key; symmetric crypto (fast) encrypts the bulk data. Pure asymmetric on gigabytes is computationally absurd; pure symmetric leaves the key-distribution problem unsolved. Understanding why the hybrid exists is understanding modern crypto design.

choices: Start digging through logs immediately — speed matters
Preserve first: isolate/preserve the system state (memory capture if warranted, disk image or snapshot), document everything, then analyze copies — never the original
Reboot to clear any malware, then investigate
Delete suspicious files to stop the bleeding
scenarios.hint: What can you never get back once it's gone — and what does analyzing the original destroy?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first move?
scenarios.situation: You suspect a server is compromised. Your instinct is to start investigating live.
scenarios.title: Don't touch that
scenarios.why: Every action on a live suspect system alters evidence — and rebooting destroys memory-resident artifacts entirely. Forensics discipline: preserve (memory first per order of volatility, then disk image), document the chain of custody, and analyze copies. You can always investigate later; you can never un-reboot.

choices: CPU and disk — the usual suspects
Volatile first: memory, network connections, running processes, logged-in users — then disk artifacts; volatile data disappears on shutdown
Only disk images matter
Check the backups first
scenarios.hint: What evidence has the shortest lifespan?
scenarios.prompt: In what order do you collect?
scenarios.situation: You have 10 minutes of access to a suspected-compromised running server before it must be taken offline.
scenarios.title: Ten minutes of truth
scenarios.why: Order of volatility governs triage: registers/cache → memory → network state → running processes → disk → logs → backups. With 10 minutes, you grab what's about to vanish: memory image, netstat/ss output, process list, logged-in users. Disk forensics can wait — the disk will still be there after shutdown; the memory won't.

choices: The file's content proves when it was created
Check all three timestamps (mtime/atime/ctime) plus journal/log evidence — timestomping is trivial, so any single timestamp is untrusted
Timestamps can't be faked on Linux
Only ctime matters
scenarios.hint: Which timestamp did the attacker forget to fake — and what does that tell you?
scenarios.prompt: What do these timestamps tell you?
scenarios.situation: A suspicious binary has atime/mtime of 2026-01-01 but ctime of today.
scenarios.title: The lying clock
scenarios.why: The mismatch is the tell: atime/mtime are trivially set with touch, but ctime (inode change time) updates on any metadata change and can't be set arbitrarily — today's ctime exposes the timestomping. Forensic timestamp analysis cross-references all three plus external sources (logs, journal). One timestamp is a claim; corroborated timestamps are evidence.

choices: Nothing — deleted is deleted
The data often remains on disk until overwritten: image the disk, use carving tools on the image, and check backups and logs for what the file contained
Run undelete on the live system repeatedly
Deleted files are always fully recoverable
scenarios.hint: What does 'delete' actually do on most filesystems — and what doesn't it do?
scenarios.prompt: What are the realistic recovery options?
scenarios.situation: An attacker deleted the access logs. You need to know what was in them.
scenarios.title: The deleted logs
scenarios.why: Deletion usually just unlinks the inode — the blocks remain until reused. Recovery means: stop writing to that disk immediately (image it), carve the image for log-format data, and check log forwarding/SIEM copies (attackers forget the remote copy). But recovery is never guaranteed — which is why centralized, tamper-evident logging is the real defense.

choices: The logs on the suspect machine — they're complete
Correlate: firewall/proxy/DNS logs, authentication logs from the domain controller, and SIEM copies — the attacker may have cleaned local logs but rarely owns every source
Just ask the user what happened
Logs are useless after a compromise
scenarios.hint: If you were the attacker, which logs would you clean — and which ones can't you reach?
scenarios.prompt: Where do you look for the truth?
scenarios.situation: Local auth logs on the suspect host have a suspicious 3-hour gap.
scenarios.title: The missing three hours
scenarios.why: Anti-forensics usually covers the attacker's reach — local logs — but not the infrastructure: the DC saw the logons, the firewall saw the connections, the proxy saw the URLs, the SIEM has forwarded copies. Correlating independent sources rebuilds the gap and often reveals the cleanup itself as evidence. Defense in depth applies to logging too.

choices: Write your findings in a chat message — it's faster
Maintain chain of custody: document who collected what, when, how (tool versions, hashes), store images securely with hashes, and keep notes contemporaneous
Chain of custody only matters for police
Hashes are optional if you trust your team
scenarios.hint: What makes your evidence believable to someone who wasn't there — six months from now?
scenarios.prompt: What does defensible evidence handling require?
scenarios.situation: Your investigation might end up in front of HR, legal, or law enforcement.
scenarios.title: Making it hold up
scenarios.why: Evidence is only as strong as its handling story: cryptographic hashes prove the image hasn't changed since collection, contemporaneous notes prove what you did, and access logs prove who touched it. This isn't just for court — HR actions and insurance claims need the same rigor. 'Trust me, I imaged it' is not a chain of custody.

choices: Patch everything instantly — speed is the only metric
Think in attack paths: which exposures chain toward your crown jewels, and which controls break those chains — prioritize by path, not by CVE count
Only fix criticals
Outsource it all to the EDR vendor
scenarios.hint: If you can only fix three things this week, how do you pick the three that matter?
scenarios.prompt: How does a defensive mindset prioritize?
scenarios.situation: Your scan shows 500 vulnerabilities. You have one week and a small team.
scenarios.title: Five hundred problems
scenarios.why: Attackers don't exploit CVEs at random — they chain exposures toward objectives. Defensive prioritization maps attack paths to crown jewels (internet → DMZ → creds → domain) and breaks the chains at the cheapest links (MFA, segmentation, patching the pivot points). CVE-count prioritization burns weeks on unreachable printers while the domain falls.

choices: Design as if breach is inevitable: segment, monitor internal traffic, limit lateral movement, and practice detection — perimeter-only defense assumes the wall never falls
Build a taller firewall and declare victory
Assume breach means you've already failed
Internal monitoring is spying on employees
scenarios.hint: What do all the major breaches of the last decade have in common about the perimeter?
scenarios.prompt: What does 'assume breach' change about your architecture?
scenarios.situation: Leadership believes the new next-gen firewall means the internal network can stay flat and unmonitored.
scenarios.title: Beyond the wall
scenarios.why: Every major breach involved a bypassed perimeter — phishing, vendor access, misconfig. Assume-breach doesn't mean defeat; it means designing so one failure isn't total: segmentation contains, internal monitoring detects, least privilege limits blast radius. The firewall is one layer, not the strategy.

choices: Give everyone admin — it speeds up work
Apply least privilege everywhere, including for yourself: use unprivileged accounts daily, elevate only for specific tasks, and regularly review who has what
Least privilege is only for interns
Review access annually whether needed or not
scenarios.hint: What did the last three privilege-escalation incidents have in common about the starting account?
scenarios.prompt: What does least privilege look like in practice?
scenarios.situation: Everyone on the IT team runs as domain admin 'because it's easier.'
scenarios.title: Admins everywhere
scenarios.why: Every over-privileged account is a pre-escalated foothold — attackers don't need exploits when they land on domain admin. Practice means: daily-driver unprivileged accounts, just-in-time elevation, and access reviews that actually revoke. Convenience is the enemy; the friction is the security.

choices: Test on the production network — it's the most realistic
Build an isolated lab (VMs, snapshots, host-only networking), get written authorization for anything shared, and never let lab malware touch real networks
Labs are a waste of time — read writeups instead
Use the corporate VPN as your lab network
scenarios.hint: What separates practice from an incident?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe, ethical way to practice offensive techniques?
scenarios.situation: You want to practice the attack techniques you're learning, to understand them as a defender.
scenarios.title: Practice without peril
scenarios.why: Understanding attacks makes you a better defender — but only with containment: isolated VMs with snapshots, host-only networks, and zero path to production or the internet for anything malicious. Written authorization covers shared environments. The line between 'practicing' and 'incident' is entirely about isolation and permission.

choices: Wipe and rebuild immediately — fastest recovery
Scope first (what's affected?), preserve evidence, contain (isolate), then eradicate and recover from known-good — wiping first destroys the 'how' and may miss persistence elsewhere
Pay any ransom to save time
Rebuild from the infected backup — it's fastest
scenarios.hint: What do you lose by wiping in the first hour — and what might survive the wipe?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct sequence?
scenarios.situation: Monday morning: ransomware on three workstations, spreading.
scenarios.title: Monday morning malware
scenarios.why: Panic-wiping feels productive but destroys evidence of patient zero and the entry vector — and if the attacker has other persistence (stolen creds, scheduled tasks on servers), the fresh builds get re-encrypted. Discipline: scope, preserve, contain, eradicate, recover from known-good media, then hunt for the entry point. Speed matters; order matters more.

choices: Security is the security team's job
Document what you did, what you changed, and why — the next person (or future you) needs the reasoning, not just the commands
Documentation slows you down — skip it
Only document failures
scenarios.hint: Six months from now, will you remember why that firewall rule exists?
scenarios.prompt: A senior admin tells you 'real hackers don't write docs.' What is the truth?
scenarios.situation: You just finished hardening a server. The senior admin says documentation is for auditors.
scenarios.title: Write it down
scenarios.why: Undocumented security is unmaintainable security: the next admin (or attacker-turned-defender) can't distinguish your deliberate controls from accidents, and can't safely change anything. Documentation is what turns one person's hardening into the organization's posture. The 'hackers don't document' myth confuses movies with operations.

lessons.title: Linux Hardening — Core concepts
concepts: SSH hardening: stale SSH keys are persistent, unaudited access — the former employee's laptop may be long gone but the key still opens root. Hardening means: inventory listeners, remove what's unneeded, bind the rest to localhost or internal interfaces, and firewall what's left.
Remote access: fix the access need properly instead of opening the file to everyone.
Least privilege: scoped rules (exact commands), personal accounts, and password-required sudo give least privilege plus attribution — and clean revocation when the internship ends.
Patch management: the overwhelming majority of exploited vulnerabilities are known CVEs with available patches — 'patch fear' is how servers get owned.

ssh-rsa AAAAB3... former-employee-laptop
ssh-rsa AAAAB3... unknown-key-2023
example.walkthrough: Stale SSH keys are persistent, unaudited access — the former employee's laptop may be long gone but the key still opens root. SSH key hygiene means: inventory keys per account, tie each to an approved identity, remove leavers promptly, and consider key expiry or certificates. 'Unknown-key-2023' on root is an incident until proven otherwise.

lessons.title: Scripting — Core concepts
concepts: Bash safety: verifying a published checksum or signature (fetched separately) before executing is the minimum due diligence. curl|bash as a habit trains you to execute uninspected code as root — the exact behavior attackers rely on.

Idempotent scripts: automation that isn't idempotent becomes a liability: duplicate firewall rules, failed user creation, unpredictable state. Cron's minimal environment (bare PATH, no shell profile) breaks scripts that work interactively — absolute paths fix that.
Principle: unquoted, unchecked variables in rm -rf are how disasters happen: an empty $BACKUP_DIR turns the command into 'rm -rf /old/*' — or worse.

example.code:
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
useradd auditor
example.walkthrough: Automation that isn't idempotent becomes a liability: duplicate firewall rules, failed user creation, unpredictable state. Check-before-change (iptables -C, id username) makes re-runs safe and convergent — the script describes desired state, not just actions. This is the foundational discipline behind all configuration management.

pitfalls: Common trap: email the log to yourself daily.
Common trap: python is safe from injection by default.
Common trap: curl the URL and pipe to bash.
Common trap: piping to bash is fine on HTTPS.

lessons.title: Cryptography Basics — Core concepts
concepts: Password hashing: hashing proves integrity and identity (this file hasn't changed); encryption provides confidentiality (only key holders can read).

Storage security: an attacker can sign anything with their own key; the security is in the key distribution (verified fingerprint, trusted introducer, prior secure exchange). Using the wrong primitive means the security property you wanted doesn't exist.
Hashing vs encryption: this confusion causes real design failures: hashed backups are still readable by everyone (hashing doesn't hide data); 'encrypted' passwords are recoverable.
Key management: real systems are hybrid: asymmetric crypto (slow, solves key distribution) exchanges a random symmetric key; symmetric crypto (fast) encrypts the bulk data.

lessons.title: Forensics Intro — Core concepts
concepts: Order of volatility: forensics discipline: preserve (memory first per order of volatility, then disk image), document the chain of custody, and analyze copies. Order of volatility governs triage: registers/cache → memory → network state → running processes → disk → logs → backups.

Evidence preservation: every action on a live suspect system alters evidence — and rebooting destroys memory-resident artifacts entirely. Evidence is only as strong as its handling story: cryptographic hashes prove the image hasn't changed since collection, contemporaneous notes prove what you did, and access logs prove who touched it.
File timestamps: one timestamp is a claim; corroborated timestamps are evidence.

Timestomping: the mismatch is the tell: atime/mtime are trivially set with touch, but ctime (inode change time) updates on any metadata change and can't be set arbitrarily — today's ctime exposes the timestomping.
File recovery: recovery means: stop writing to that disk immediately (image it), carve the image for log-format data, and check log forwarding/SIEM copies (attackers forget the remote copy).

example.walkthrough: The mismatch is the tell: atime/mtime are trivially set with touch, but ctime (inode change time) updates on any metadata change and can't be set arbitrarily — today's ctime exposes the timestomping. Forensic timestamp analysis cross-references all three plus external sources (logs, journal).

pitfalls: Common trap: chain of custody only matters for police.

Common trap: the file's content proves when it was created.

lessons.title: Hands-On Hacking Lab Concepts — Core concepts
concepts: Think like the attacker to defend like a professional: every technique here is taught so you can recognize, detect, and blunt it — practice only on lab systems you own or are authorized to test.
Linux is the attacker's home turf and the defender's: master the socket table (ss), process tree (ps), permissions including SUID, and the logs in /var/log — misconfigurations here become footholds.
Scripting turns one-off commands into repeatable analysis: a short bash loop that parses logs or checks configurations beats manual inspection at scale, for both offense and defense.
Networks trust too easily: ARP, DNS, and many legacy protocols lack authentication, so attackers spoof them — and defenders answer with switch-level validation and encrypted alternatives.
Cryptography fails in implementation, not in theory: unsalted fast hashes, hardcoded secrets, and confused encoding-versus-encryption choices are where real breaches come from.

example.walkthrough: This finds every SUID-root binary on the system — the classic privilege-escalation inventory step. Run it on a lab host, research each result, and remove the SUID bit from anything non-essential. Attackers run this exact command after gaining a foothold; defenders should run it first.

pitfalls: Common trap: practicing techniques on systems you do not own — the lab boundary is the entire difference between training and a crime.
Common trap: confusing encoding (Base64), hashing (MD5), and encryption (AES) — they solve different problems and fail differently.
Common trap: running untrusted scripts or pasting commands you do not understand — a classic way to get owned while 'learning'.
Common trap: assuming a quiet network is a safe network — scans and spoofing are often invisible without the right logging.

simulations.brief: A teammate sets a shared script to 777 'to make it work.' Walk through why this is wrong and what to do.

sections.heading: Cryptography Basics
items: Password hashing — hashing proves integrity and identity (this file hasn't changed); encryption provides confidentiality (only key holders can read).

Storage security — an attacker can sign anything with their own key; the security is in the key distribution (verified fingerprint, trusted introducer, prior secure exchange). Using the wrong primitive means the security property you wanted doesn't exist.
Hashing vs encryption — this confusion causes real design failures: hashed backups are still readable by everyone (hashing doesn't hide data); 'encrypted' passwords are recoverable.
Key management — real systems are hybrid: asymmetric crypto (slow, solves key distribution) exchanges a random symmetric key; symmetric crypto (fast) encrypts the bulk data.
Common trap — hashing is encryption with a fixed key.
Common trap — use the current timestamp as the key.
Common trap — encrypt the passwords with AES so they can be decrypted later.

sections.heading: Forensics Intro
items: Order of volatility — forensics discipline: preserve (memory first per order of volatility, then disk image), document the chain of custody, and analyze copies. Order of volatility governs triage: registers/cache → memory → network state → running processes → disk → logs → backups.

Evidence preservation — every action on a live suspect system alters evidence — and rebooting destroys memory-resident artifacts entirely. Evidence is only as strong as its handling story: cryptographic hashes prove the image hasn't changed since collection, contemporaneous notes…
File timestamps — one timestamp is a claim; corroborated timestamps are evidence.

Timestomping — the mismatch is the tell: atime/mtime are trivially set with touch, but ctime (inode change time) updates on any metadata change and can't be set arbitrarily — today's ctime exposes the timestomping.
File recovery — recovery means: stop writing to that disk immediately (image it), carve the image for log-format data, and check log forwarding/SIEM copies (attackers forget the remote copy).
Common trap — chain of custody only matters for police.

sections.heading: Defensive Mindset
items: Attack path thinking — defensive prioritization maps attack paths to crown jewels (internet → DMZ → creds → domain) and breaks the chains at the cheapest links (MFA, segmentation, patching the pivot points).
Prioritization — cVE-count prioritization burns weeks on unreachable printers while the domain falls.
Assume breach — every major breach involved a bypassed perimeter — phishing, vendor access, misconfig.
Least privilege — assume-breach doesn't mean defeat; it means designing so one failure isn't total: segmentation contains, internal monitoring detects, least privilege limits blast radius.
Common trap — assume breach means you've already failed.
